Querying with dplyr

Source: vignettes/articles/dplyr.Rmd
dplyr.Rmd

tbl(con, variable) gives a lazy table over one variable of an xarray Dataset. dplyr verbs on it accumulate, and nothing is read until collect(). The verbs compile to a single Python statement, the same kind you could write yourself for dbGetQuery(), and show_query() prints it. This article shows how each verb compiles, and so what gets read.

library(xrdbi)
library(DBI)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

The examples use a small Dataset built in Python: ten days of a sea-surface-temperature-like variable on a 1 degree grid, with latitude stored north to south, as many products store it, and a few missing values.

con <- dbConnect(xarray(), builder = function(xr) {
  reticulate::py_run_string("
import xarray as xr, numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
lat = np.arange(-40.5, -50, -1.0)            # descending
lon = np.arange(140.5, 150, 1.0)
time = pd.date_range('2026-01-01', periods=10)
sst = 12 + 0.5 * (lat[None, :, None] + 45) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, (10, 10, 10))
sst[:, 0, :2] = np.nan
toy = xr.Dataset({'sst': (('time', 'lat', 'lon'), sst.astype('float32'))},
                 coords={'time': time, 'lat': lat, 'lon': lon})
")
  reticulate::py_eval("toy", convert = FALSE)
})
con
#> <XarrayConnection>
#>   dims: time: 10, lat: 10, lon: 10
#>   vars: sst
sst <- tbl(con, "sst")

What a tbl supports

  • filter(), with ==, %in%, <, <=, >, >=, between() and & (or several arguments), each comparing a field with a value
  • select() with plain column names
  • head()
  • collect() (a tibble), as.data.frame() (a data frame), show_query(), and printing

Anything else, such as mutate(), summarise() or arrange(), has no method: collect() first, and carry on with dplyr in R. Filter forms outside the list error when the filter is added, saying which forms are supported:

try(sst |> filter(lat < -48 | lat > -42))
#> Error : unsupported filter expression: lat < -48 | lat > -42
#> supported: ==, %in%, <, <=, >, >=, between(), &

Filters on dimensions become selections

A filter on a dimension compiles to a label-based .sel(), so xarray reads only the cells in range. Inclusive bounds (>=, <=, between()) are a slice(); %in% is a list of exact labels; == is a single label.

q <- sst |> filter(between(lon, 142, 144), lat == -42.5,
                   time >= as.Date("2026-01-09"))
show_query(q)
#> ds['sst'].sel(lat=-42.5, lon=slice(142, 144), time=slice('2026-01-09', None))
collect(q)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   time                  lon   lat   sst
#>   <dttm>              <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 2026-01-09 00:00:00  142. -42.5  13.1
#> 2 2026-01-09 00:00:00  144. -42.5  13.1
#> 3 2026-01-10 00:00:00  142. -42.5  13.6
#> 4 2026-01-10 00:00:00  144. -42.5  12.9

Strict bounds (<, >) cannot be a .sel(), which is inclusive, so the statement selects the inclusive range and then trims the boundary labels with a boolean .isel(). The result is still an xarray selection, read cell for cell:

sst |> filter(lon > 141.5, lon < 144.5) |> show_query()
#> ds['sst'].sel(lon=slice(141.5, 144.5)).pipe(lambda a: a.isel(lon=(a['lon'].to_index() > 141.5) & (a['lon'].to_index() < 144.5)))

Latitude here runs north to south, and a slice() in xarray follows the order of the coordinate. Written by hand, slice(-43, -41) would select nothing. The compiler checks the direction of each filtered dimension and writes the slice in its order:

q <- sst |> filter(lat >= -43, lat <= -41, time == as.Date("2026-01-01"))
show_query(q)
#> ds['sst'].sel(lat=slice(-41, -43), time='2026-01-01')
collect(q)
#> # A tibble: 20 × 4
#>      lat   lon time                  sst
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dttm>              <dbl>
#>  1 -41.5  140. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.8
#>  2 -41.5  142. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.9
#>  3 -41.5  142. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.5
#>  4 -41.5  144. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.7
#>  5 -41.5  144. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.6
#>  6 -41.5  146. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.9
#>  7 -41.5  146. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.8
#>  8 -41.5  148. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.7
#>  9 -41.5  148. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.5
#> 10 -41.5  150. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.7
#> 11 -42.5  140. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.3
#> 12 -42.5  142. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.2
#> 13 -42.5  142. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.6
#> 14 -42.5  144. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.6
#> 15 -42.5  144. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  12.4
#> 16 -42.5  146. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  12.7
#> 17 -42.5  146. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.2
#> 18 -42.5  148. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.1
#> 19 -42.5  148. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.3
#> 20 -42.5  150. 2026-01-01 00:00:00  13.3

Dates and times compile to their instant in UTC, the way xarray stores times: a Date as 'YYYY-MM-DD', a POSIXct as 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS', whatever its time zone.

sst |>
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("2026-01-05 10:00", tz = "Australia/Hobart")) |>
  show_query()
#> ds['sst'].sel(time=slice('2026-01-04T23:00:00', None))

Filters on values run in Python after the selection

A filter on the variable itself cannot be a selection, because which cells pass depends on their values. It becomes a pandas .query() on the selected cells, before they come to R. The dimension filters still narrow what is read first:

q <- sst |> filter(lat <= -48, sst > 10.4)
show_query(q)
#> ds['sst'].sel(lat=slice(-48, None)).pipe(_xrdbi_render).query('`sst` > 10.4')
collect(q)
#> # A tibble: 34 × 4
#>    time                  lat   lon   sst
#>    <dttm>              <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 2026-01-01 00:00:00 -48.5  140.  10.5
#>  2 2026-01-01 00:00:00 -48.5  144.  10.5
#>  3 2026-01-01 00:00:00 -48.5  146.  10.5
#>  4 2026-01-02 00:00:00 -48.5  144.  11.1
#>  5 2026-01-02 00:00:00 -48.5  144.  10.5
#>  6 2026-01-03 00:00:00 -48.5  140.  10.5
#>  7 2026-01-04 00:00:00 -48.5  142.  10.7
#>  8 2026-01-04 00:00:00 -48.5  144.  10.5
#>  9 2026-01-04 00:00:00 -48.5  148.  10.6
#> 10 2026-01-04 00:00:00 -48.5  148.  10.4
#> # ℹ 24 more rows

With such a filter in place, select() and head() run in pandas too, so only the rows and columns asked for cross to R.

sst |> filter(sst > 14) |> select(time, lat, sst) |> head(3) |> show_query()
#> ds['sst'].pipe(_xrdbi_render).query('`sst` > 14')[['time', 'lat', 'sst']].head(3)

Missing values are NaN in the array and stay NaN in R. A value comparison is false for them, so they drop out:

nrow(collect(sst |> filter(time == as.Date("2026-01-01"), lat == -40.5)))
#> [1] 10
nrow(collect(sst |> filter(time == as.Date("2026-01-01"), lat == -40.5,
                           sst > 0)))
#> [1] 8

Filters on non-dimension coordinates, such as the 2-D longitude and latitude of a curvilinear grid, are also exact pandas filters, but the read is first narrowed to the block of the grid that holds every passing cell. The curvilinear grids article shows it.

head() reads one corner

Without a value filter, head(n) and select() apply in R to the fetched rows, and head(n) first narrows the selection to the leading block of the array that holds its n rows. The rows of the long form run in C order, the last dimension fastest, so the first n rows are a corner of the array:

sst |> head(4) |> show_query()
#> ds['sst'].isel(time=slice(0, 1), lat=slice(0, 1), lon=slice(0, 4)) 
#> # then in R: head(4)

That matters on big stores. This is the ARCO ERA5 reanalysis on Google Cloud, an hourly zarr store with a time axis of over a million steps. The first rows of a variable are one chunk’s worth of reading:

reticulate::py_require(c("zarr", "gcsfs"))
era <- dbConnect(xarray(),
  "gs://gcp-public-data-arco-era5/ar/full_37-1h-0p25deg-chunk-1.zarr-v3",
  engine = "zarr", storage_options = reticulate::dict(token = "anon"))
dbGetInfo(era)$sizes$time
#> [1] 1323648

t2m <- tbl(era, "2m_temperature") |>
  filter(time >= as.POSIXct("1980-01-01", tz = "UTC")) |>
  select(time, latitude, longitude, `2m_temperature`) |>
  head(3)
show_query(t2m)
#> ds['2m_temperature'].sel(time=slice('1980-01-01T00:00:00', None)).isel(time=slice(0, 1), latitude=slice(0, 1), longitude=slice(0, 3)) 
#> # then in R: head(3) |> select(time, latitude, longitude, `2m_temperature`)
collect(t2m)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   time                latitude longitude `2m_temperature`
#>   <dttm>                 <dbl>     <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1 1980-01-01 00:00:00       90      0                248.
#> 2 1980-01-01 00:00:00       90      0.25             248.
#> 3 1980-01-01 00:00:00       90      0.5              248.
dbDisconnect(era)

Printing is a preview

Printing a lazy table shows the compiled statement, the sizes it selects, and its first rows, reading at most one chunk. options(xrdbi.print_n = ) sets the number of rows, and options(xrdbi.print_preview = FALSE) turns the preview off.

sst |> filter(lat <= -45)
#> <tbl_xarray> sst
#>   python: ds['sst'].sel(lat=slice(-45, None))
#>   sizes : time: 10, lat:  5, lon: 10
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   time                  lat   lon   sst
#>   <dttm>              <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 2026-01-01 00:00:00 -45.5  140.  11.8
#> 2 2026-01-01 00:00:00 -45.5  142.  11.5
#> 3 2026-01-01 00:00:00 -45.5  142.  12.0
#> 4 2026-01-01 00:00:00 -45.5  144.  11.6
#> 5 2026-01-01 00:00:00 -45.5  144.  12.0
#> 6 2026-01-01 00:00:00 -45.5  146.  11.4
#> # lazy preview of the first cells (reads at most one chunk); collect() for the full result

The guard

collect() sizes the xarray part of the statement before reading it, and errors above max_cells cells (10 million by default, or getOption("xrdbi.max_cells")). Pass force = TRUE to read anyway, or filter more dimensions. Here the limit is set low to show it:

try(collect(sst, max_cells = 500))
#> Error : collect would materialize 1,000 cells, over the guard (500); constrain more dimensions (e.g. a time range), raise options(xrdbi.max_cells=), or collect(force = TRUE)
nrow(collect(sst, max_cells = 500, force = TRUE))
#> [1] 1000
dbDisconnect(con)
